stem: A medication error is intercepted before it reaches the client. Why is reporting this near miss useful for patient safety?

options.A: A near miss confirms that existing safety controls are adequate, so additional review would add little useful information.
options.B: Reporting the near miss can reveal contributing factors and system weaknesses before a similar event causes client harm.
options.C: Near-miss reporting is useful mainly to identify which individual should be disciplined when no client harm occurred.
options.D: Safety reporting should be limited to events that cause injury because intercepted errors cannot provide meaningful learning.

rationale: AHRQ describes near misses or close calls as safety events in which an error is detected or does not reach the patient before harm occurs. Near-miss reporting and analysis can identify contributing human, technical, process, and organizational factors and reveal weaknesses in care systems before a similar event results in harm. AHRQ's systems approach to event investigation states that the objective of analyzing adverse events and near misses is preventing future adverse events rather than assigning blame. Therefore B is correct. A incorrectly assumes interception proves the system is adequate, C misuses reporting as a primarily punitive tool, and D discards an important source of safety learning.
educational_objective: Report and analyze near misses because intercepted errors can expose contributing factors and latent system weaknesses that can be corrected before future patient harm occurs.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_document_title: System-Focused Event Investigation and Analysis Guide; Implementing Near-Miss Reporting and Improvement Tracking; Patient Safety Event Reporting
source_version_date: Current AHRQ patient-safety guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: CANDOR System-Focused Event Investigation and Analysis Guide > A Systems Approach: objective of investigating an adverse event or near miss is prevention of future events, not blame; focus on process/system factors. AHRQ near-miss reporting guidance: near misses are detected/corrected before harm and reporting/analysis is vital to understanding and correcting delivery-system weaknesses. Event-reporting guidance includes near-miss/close-call events and contributory factors.
source_claim_supported: Reporting an intercepted medication near miss can expose contributing factors and system weaknesses and support preventive improvement before a similar event harms a patient; the purpose is learning/prevention rather than blame.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Management of Care: participate in quality-improvement activities, report safety events/near misses according to policy, analyze system factors, and implement measures to improve client safety.
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — near-miss reporting and patient-safety improvement

source_original.stem: A medication error is intercepted before it reaches the client. Why is reporting this near miss useful for patient safety?

options.A: A near miss confirms that existing safety controls are adequate, so additional review can distort performance data.
options.B: Reporting the near miss can reveal contributing factors and system weaknesses before a similar event causes patient harm.
options.C: Near misses are useful mainly for identifying which individual should be disciplined when no patient harm occurred.
options.D: Safety reporting should be limited to events that cause injury because no learning can come from intercepted errors.

source_original.rationale: AHRQ defines a near miss as an error that could have caused harm under different circumstances but was intercepted or did not harm the patient. Patient-safety reporting systems collect near misses so they can be analyzed along with other safety events and used to identify contributing factors and improvement opportunities.
source_original.source_detail: Near misses are reportable safety events and can be analyzed for contributing factors Source has no separate formal version identifier in the cited page metadata; live currentness and applicability rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: prioritization, assignment/delegation, advocacy/client rights, continuity/referral, legal scope, professional limitations and emergency/quality-management activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the near-miss learning construct and key B, grounded the rationale in AHRQ's current systems-based event-analysis guidance, strengthened the nonpunitive prevention framing, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a defined patient-safety principle.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current AHRQ patient-safety/event-analysis guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: AHRQ CANDOR, reporting and near-miss guidance live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: AHRQ CANDOR Guide 4 > A Systems Approach; near-miss reporting/improvement guidance; event-reporting contributory-factor sections
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately frames the event as intercepted before reaching the client and focuses on system learning/prevention rather than using voluntary reporting to calculate event rates or assign automatic blame.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because interception does not prove the system is adequate and a near miss can reveal latent weaknesses.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because system-focused event analysis is intended to prevent recurrence, not primarily identify someone to punish.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because near misses are specifically useful safety events for learning and improvement despite absence of harm.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B states the recognized safety-learning value of a near miss without adding a punitive or no-learning assumption.
audit_findings.cueing: All options explain the purpose/value of reporting the same intercepted error.
audit_findings.blueprint: Management of Care — quality improvement, event reporting and systems-based patient safety.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current AHRQ systems-analysis and near-miss reporting guidance, all options, rationale, objective, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN Management of Care alignment. B remained uniquely correct.
